payload.rationale: The most recent observed data (supplied record) show U-3 at 4.1% in August and July 2026, 4.2% in June, with August payrolls +162k. For YES, the September reading must print at least 4.5% at one-decimal precision — a 0.4 pp jump in a single month. Historically, month-to-month changes in the U-3 rate of 0.4 pp or more essentially occur only during recessions or major shocks (e.g., 2008-09, 2020); outside such episodes, moves are almost always within ±0.2 pp. Absent evidence of an acute shock between the August survey and the September reference week, the base rate for a 0.4 pp jump is on the order of 1-3%. I also allow slightly for the weak June/July revised payroll figures (31k, 21k) signaling underlying softening, and for unknown developments after the 2026-09-18 information cutoff, which nudges the estimate up marginally. Too high: a 0.4 pp one-month jump from a stable 4.1% base is extraordinarily rare, and the payroll rebound in August argues against imminent deterioration; the true chance could be nearer 1%. Too low: the supplied packet is thin; I cannot observe weekly claims, consumer surveys, or any shock (financial stress, policy event, disaster, government disruption affecting data collection) occurring in late September that could produce an outsized move or an anomalous print; labor force participation swings can also add noise to the household-survey rate. Rounding cuts both ways but the threshold requires a full 4.5% print.
limitations: Only three monthly readings supplied; no weekly claims, participation, or high-frequency indicators available.
No information on events after 2026-09-18 that could affect the September reference-week survey.
Base-rate reasoning relies on general historical knowledge of U-3 monthly volatility, not a supplied transition dataset.
Possibility of release delay or data anomalies not assessed.
